cap.1: Circle 12 December 2026. Your talk that day, plus turning up to 11 of the 14 Saturdays, is what passing this course means.
cap.2: The pass condition has two parts: attend at least 11 of the 14 Saturday sessions, and give the final talk on 12 December 2026, the W14 Saturday.
cap.3: Pass = attended ≥ 11 of 14 Saturdays, and the final presentation given on 12 December 2026 (W14). The talk reports your capstone: one question, answered over W12 to W14.

cap.1: Think of it as a gig where you play one song you already know, all the way through. Not a medley, and not a song you learned that morning.
cap.2: The capstone is one question, small enough to answer in three Saturdays, using a technique you've already implemented. The talk is you playing that one song for the room.
cap.3: Scope is the whole game: one question, one technique you've already made work, one answer. The talk presents that answer, not a survey of everything you could have tried.

chapters.name: The three Saturdays
chapters.title: From first check-in to the talk

cap.1: The check-ins about your project start in week 8. Weeks 12, 13 and 14 are project time, and the talk lands on the last of them.
cap.2: Three Saturdays, not one: W12 is already project time. /checkpoint starts asking at W8, so pick the question well before the first project Saturday.
cap.3: W8 (31 Oct): check-ins begin. W12 (28 Nov) and W13 (5 Dec): project Saturdays. W14 (12 Dec): project time and the talk. Plan to have the answer before the last one.

chapters.verdict: The projects that finish reuse a technique from a Saturday you actually did.

cap.1: Learning a brand-new song for the gig is tempting. The projects that finish reuse something you already built, on a Saturday you actually did.
cap.2: Scope it against what you already built: activation patching, an SAE latent study, a small eval. A new technique started in W12 splits three Saturdays between learning it and using it.
cap.3: A technique you've already implemented comes with working code and known failure modes, so the three Saturdays go on the question itself, not on making the method run.

cap.1: A clear talk follows the song: the question, the technique you used, what you found, how sure you are, and what it means. One path, start to finish.
cap.2: Open with the one question and why it matters. Show the technique only as far as the result needs, then spend your time on what you found and how far it goes.
cap.3: State the answer with its scope: the model, the prompts or data, what the technique can and can't rule out. A finding reported with its limits is one others can build on.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Built on what you already made
Explaining a finding lets others act on it

cap.1: Understanding AI only helps steer it once you can explain what you found. Your talk is the first time your own finding about a model leaves your laptop.
cap.2: Weeks of techniques end in one question you can answer and explain. That habit, a small scope and a clear answer, is how interpretability and evals work gets used.
cap.3: Communicating a result with its scope and uncertainty is part of the research: a finding about a model only steers anything once others can check it and build on it.

coda.title: Your 14 Saturdays: click one to mark it missed

caption.1: Each square is a Saturday: top row weeks 1 to 7, bottom row 8 to 14. Click to mark one missed. How many can you miss before you drop below the line?
caption.2: Attendance needs 11 of the 14 Saturdays, and the talk on 12 December is the last square. Missing a project Saturday costs twice: attendance and project time.
caption.3: Pass = at least 11 of 14 attended, and the talk given. Three misses is the whole margin, so spend it on purpose; W12 and W13 are project Saturdays and W14 carries the talk.

hamming.what: The talk on 12 December 2026 that, with 11 of 14 Saturdays attended, is the pass condition: one question, answered with a technique you've already built.
hamming.when: Pick the question before W12, since /checkpoint starts asking at W8, and work on it across three Saturdays, W12 to W14.
hamming.why: A small question answered clearly is the project that finishes, and explaining what you found is how understanding a model becomes something others can use.

object.title: The talk on a thread
object.subtitle: Each block is a part of your talk; the thread running through them all is your one question.

cap.1: Your talk as blocks on one thread. The thread is your question: every block should hang on it, or it doesn't belong in the talk.
cap.2: Each block is a part of the talk; the tube through them is the single question. A slide that doesn't connect to it is a candidate to cut.
cap.3: Structure follows scope: one question threads the whole talk, so each section must carry evidence for its answer or the context needed to read it.

cap.1: The tallest block is what you found. That's where the room's attention, and most of your time, should go.
cap.2: Spend the most time on the result and how you got it, using a technique you'd already built, rather than on long background.
cap.3: Allocate time by information: the result and its uncertainty carry the talk; the method gets as much as the result needs to be believed.

cap.1: Right beside the result sits 'how sure you are'. A finding without its limits is only half a finding.
cap.2: Name the limits: the model you used, the prompts or data you tested, and what your technique can't rule out.
cap.3: Report scope and uncertainty explicitly: model, data, technique, and the alternative explanations your experiment doesn't exclude.

cap.1: From above it's a short string: one question, five blocks. Small enough to answer in three Saturdays is small enough to explain.
cap.2: Three Saturdays, W12 to W14, bound the project; a talk built on one question fits inside that.
cap.3: Scope for the time available: one question you can answer with a technique you've implemented is the project that finishes.

cap.1: Up close, the first block: say your question in one sentence. If you can't yet, that's what /checkpoint will be asking about from week 8.
cap.2: A one-sentence question is the test of scope. /checkpoint starts asking at W8, well before project time begins at W12.
cap.3: If the question can't be stated in a sentence, the project isn't scoped; fix that before W12, while there's still time to choose.
